The release also adds a span and session filter-expression reference and refreshes built-in model token prices, with a 20.2.1 patch the next day doing another price update and a client 3.2.0 adding POST /traces/transfer.

tail.title: Langfuse 4.11.0 tells the truth about observations past the load cap
tail.summary: v4.11.0 fixes traces silently hiding observations beyond the UI load cap, which previously made a long trace look complete when it was not — a real hazard if you were eyeballing agent traces for missing steps. It also exposes v4 migration observation evidence, makes the markdown render character limit configurable, shows existing annotation counts on sessions, lets viewer-role users use Ask AI, and recovers OpenRouter error provenance in evals.

tail.title: Qwen Code 0.21.12 adds a diff-growth brake to stop autofix from ballooning a patch
tail.summary: The release adds a configurable per-window budget capping how many source and test lines an autofix review may add, plus workspace file uploads to the Web Shell composer by drag-and-drop or the @ panel with progress tracking, and makes confirmed Critical findings mandatory rather than advisory. Note that this repo also publishes internal CI benchmark runs as GitHub releases (titles like 'DSW EAS SWE + Terminal-Bench E2E r3'), which are not releases and should be filtered out of any atom sweep.

tail.title: Anthropic SDK for Python 0.122.0 adds output_behavior to dream creation
tail.summary: v0.122.0 adds an output_behavior parameter to dream creation, choosing between creating a new memory store and updating the input store in place. It also runs AWS SigV4 signing off the event loop in async Bedrock clients, which removes a blocking call from the async path, and exposes beta.messages.parse and streaming on Bedrock.

tail.title: Claude Agent SDK for Python tracks the CLI to 2.1.233
tail.summary: v0.2.139 bundles Claude CLI 2.1.233 and v0.2.138 bundles 2.1.232, so SDK-driven agents pick up default subagent forking, the cross-session @-mention routing and the Linux Bash memory cgroup without a separate CLI install. The TypeScript SDK shipped matching v0.3.232 and v0.3.233.

tail.title: LangChain's OpenAI integration moves to the OpenAI 3.0 SDK
tail.summary: langchain-openai 1.5.0 adds support for the OpenAI 3.0 Python SDK, a major-version bump that anyone pinning the underlying client will need to reconcile. A 1.5.1 the next day fixes streamed encrypted reasoning being dropped, and langchain-openrouter 0.2.8 fixes cost metadata being lost from usage chunks — worth noting if you compute OpenRouter spend from LangChain callbacks.

tail.title: CrewAI 1.15.16 adds execution-context management with UUIDs
tail.summary: The release introduces UUID-based execution context management, records which exception kind ended a flow, and records the running release on every emitted span, all of which make failed multi-agent runs attributable after the fact. It also fixes a failed turn incorrectly marking the next turn as failed, and adds frontend guides for CopilotKit and AG-UI.

tail.title: opencode 1.18.18 fixes Kimi prompt selection and xAI xhigh reasoning effort
tail.summary: A small correctness release: opencode was selecting the wrong system prompt for the official Moonshot and Kimi providers, and the xhigh reasoning effort setting was not reaching xAI models. Both are the kind of silent misconfiguration that degrades output without erroring.

tail.title: Gemini CLI nightly adds a tool-call formatter and failure summaries to its eval harness
tail.summary: The 13 August nightly lands eval validation plus a tool-call formatter integrated with failure summaries, making the CLI's own evaluation output readable rather than raw. The following night's build adds context-aware silent retries with an availability TTL for capacity errors, and rolls back an entire multi-turn request on cancellation or abort instead of leaving a half-applied turn.

tail.title: OpenRouter doubles the web_search surcharge on Gemini and GPT-5.6 Luna/Terra
tail.summary: An overnight diff of the full OpenRouter catalog against yesterday's snapshot shows the web_search price going 0.007 to 0.014 on Gemini 3.7 Flash, its batch variant and gemini-flash-latest, and 0.005 to 0.01 on all four GPT-5.6 Luna, Luna Pro, Terra and Terra Pro entries. Base token pricing on those models did not move. Anyone whose agent loop calls the built-in web search on every turn just had that line item double with no announcement.

tail.title: Z.ai's price ladder inverts overnight: GLM 5.2 rises again while GLM 5 falls 37%
tail.summary: In a single overnight diff GLM 5.2 went from $1.98 to $3.74 per million output tokens (input $0.63 to $1.19, cached input $0.0945 to $0.221) while the older GLM 5 moved the opposite way, $2.55 to $1.92 output and $0.95 to $0.60 input with cached input down 40% to $0.12. This is GLM 5.2's second rise in four days on top of the 7.6x jump recorded on 11 August, putting the cumulative move near 17x from its introductory price. The result is an inversion worth checking before you pin a model string: the previous-generation GLM 5 is now roughly half the price of the newer 5.2 rather than modestly below it.

tail.title: Kimi K2.6 cuts output pricing 41% overnight
tail.summary: Kimi K2.6 went from $4.00 to $2.36 per million output tokens and $0.95 to $0.5605 per million input, with cached input down to $0.0944. Sibling model Kimi K2.7 Code moved the other way but only marginally ($3.40 to $3.50 out). The cut lands the week after Sakana built its Japanese-specialised Namazu API on K2.6, which is now materially cheaper to run against.

tail.title: Qwen3.5-397B-A17B drops output pricing 35% while the 35B-A3B raises it 44%
tail.summary: The big Qwen3.5 MoE went from $3.60 to $2.34 per million output and $0.50 to $0.39 input, but lost its cached-input rate entirely (it now reports none). The small 35B-A3B moved the opposite way, output $1.25 to $1.80 even as input fell $0.25 to $0.225. Combined with the Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B context listing quietly changing from 1,010,000 to 1,048,576, the Qwen line saw four separate uncommunicated catalog edits in one night.

tail.title: Llama 4 Maverick's completion price ticks up 15%
tail.summary: Maverick went from $0.696 to $0.80 per million completion tokens with input unchanged, the only Meta model to move in the overnight diff. Small in absolute terms, but it is a rise on a model whose main selling point was cost, in a week when Meta's newer Muse line took the open-weight attention.

tail.title: Grok 4.6 lands in GitHub Copilot two days after release
tail.summary: xAI's news index lists a 14 August post putting Grok 4.6 inside GitHub Copilot, following the 12 August Grok 4.6 launch that emphasised long-running agents and interactive visual work. Distribution rather than capability news, but it is the fastest xAI-to-Copilot turnaround so far and gives the model a coding-agent surface it did not have at launch.

tail.title: Baseten adds DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 to its model APIs
tail.summary: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 is now callable through Baseten's OpenAI-compatible endpoint as deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, one day after the open weights landed. Baseten has been the fastest of the serving providers to pick up new open releases this month (Inkling Small on 30 July, Kimi K3 on 27 July), which makes its changelog a useful early signal for which open models are practically servable rather than merely downloadable.

tail.title: An INT8 W8A16 Qwen3.8-27B with the MTP head preserved for vLLM
tail.summary: This compressed-tensors conversion keeps weights at INT8 and activations at 16-bit while explicitly preserving the multi-token-prediction head, which most community quants drop. That matters because Qwen3.8-27B ships MTP for speculative decoding, and a quant that discards the head silently forfeits the speedup. A companion NVFP4+MTP conversion for Blackwell cards landed the same day from sakamakismile.

tail.title: ggml-org publishes its own Qwen3.8-27B GGUF, confirming upstream llama.cpp support
tail.summary: The llama.cpp maintainers' own org published a Qwen3.8-27B GGUF on 14 August, which is the practical confirmation that the Gated DeltaNet hybrid plus vision projector converts and runs on stock llama.cpp rather than needing a fork. lmstudio-community shipped both GGUF and MLX-4bit builds the same afternoon, and bartowski's conversion is at 27 likes.

tail.title: ubergarm ships an ik_llama.cpp imatrix build of Qwen3.8-27B
tail.summary: An importance-matrix quantization targeting the ik_llama.cpp fork, which carries quant types and CPU kernels that upstream does not. For a 27B on a 16GB card the ik fork's SOTA sub-4-bit types are the difference between a Q3 that degrades noticeably and one that mostly does not, so this is the build worth benchmarking against the mainline Q3_K_M rather than assuming they are equivalent.

tail.title: LTX-2.5 gains a multi-subject reference LoRA for consistent characters across shots
tail.summary: A community fine-tune of Lightricks' LTX-2.5 that conditions image-to-video generation on several reference subjects at once, which is the piece needed to keep two or more characters recognisable across separate generated shots. LTX-2.5 is the video model explicitly tuned for consumer RTX cards, so this runs on Patrick's stack via ComfyUI rather than needing rented compute.

tail.title: Sakana updates Sakana Chat with Fugu and a new-generation Namazu
tail.summary: Sakana's Japanese-language blog announced that Sakana Chat now serves both the Fugu orchestration model and a new-generation Namazu, three days after the company showed Fugu's conductor retrained on Gemma 4 to demonstrate that its orchestration layer does not depend on the base model. Namazu is the Japanese-specialised reasoning model built on Kimi K2.6 that reached OpenRouter on 11 August.

tail.title: Cline's CLI stops auto-updating out from under a live session
tail.summary: CLI 3.0.55 defers auto-updates while a CLI is attached to the Hub: the update is recorded at startup and installed on exit once the Hub confirms nothing else is attached, because a background update was previously swapping the package out mid-session and killing it with 'Hub connection closed (code=1006)'. It also defuses a worse path in CLI 3.0.54 and earlier, whose updater restarted the Hub mid-session and then rejected every replacement, bricking the running session. If you script long unattended agent runs, this is the fix that stops them dying at random.

tail.title: An MLX build of Qwen3.8-27B tuned specifically for its speculative-decoding head
tail.summary: Three MTPLX variants (Optimized-Speed at 23 likes, Optimized-Quality at 13, Bare-Speed at 6) target Apple Silicon and keep Qwen3.8-27B's multi-token-prediction head wired for speculative decoding, splitting the speed/quality tradeoff into separate checkpoints rather than one compromise. The three-way split is a useful published ablation on the same base: it is rare to get speed-tuned and quality-tuned conversions of one model from one author on the same day.

tail.title: A token-efficiency-tuned Qwen3.8-27B GGUF arrives with the MTP head intact
tail.summary: Tagged for llama.cpp with mtp, speculative-decoding and token-efficient, this is one of the few community Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs that advertises preserving the multi-token-prediction path rather than flattening it during conversion. Given that roughly twenty independent Qwen3.8-27B quants appeared inside 48 hours, MTP preservation is the axis actually worth sorting on before download size.

tail.title: An uncensored Qwen3.8-27B GGUF lands within 20 hours of the base weights
tail.summary: At 21 likes this is the most-liked of the refusal-modified Qwen3.8-27B builds, an imatrix GGUF that also keeps the MTP and speculative-decoding path. Paired with the four abliterated variants of the same base from the same 30-hour window, there is now a set of independently-produced safety-stripped checkpoints over identical weights, which is the controlled comparison an abliteration study normally has to construct by hand.

tail.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron teacher family covers competition coding and instruction following as separate checkpoints
tail.summary: Beyond the STEM teacher, NVIDIA released Competition-Coding, Instruction-Following, General-Reasoning and Chat variants of the same 550B LatentMoE architecture within minutes of each other. Publishing the teachers separately rather than only the distilled students is unusual and makes the Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation recipe auditable: you can in principle check what each teacher contributed instead of taking the student's benchmark line on faith.

tail.title: LiteLLM signs every Docker image with cosign and pins the key by commit hash
tail.summary: The v1.98.0 dev line documents cosign verification for all LiteLLM images, recommending verification against the signing key pinned to an immutable commit hash rather than the release tag, since tag protection is a weaker guarantee than a hash. Functional changes include attributing Vertex passthrough batch cost to the right key/team/tags and scoping file-list pagination cursors to the caller — the latter being a cross-tenant leak in a multi-user proxy.

tail.title: Gemini CLI adds context-aware silent retries with an availability TTL for capacity errors
tail.summary: The 14 August nightly makes capacity errors retry silently with awareness of the request context and caches model availability behind a TTL, so a transient 'no capacity' no longer surfaces as a hard failure. It also rolls back an entire multi-turn request on cancellation or abort rather than leaving a partially-applied turn in history, which is the failure mode that quietly corrupts an agent transcript.

tail.title: LangChain's OpenRouter integration was dropping cost metadata from usage chunks
tail.summary: langchain-openrouter 0.2.8 fixes cost metadata being lost from streamed usage chunks, meaning any spend accounting built on LangChain callbacks over OpenRouter was undercounting on streamed calls. The release also refreshes model profile data three times over, which is how the package tracks OpenRouter's frequently-changing catalog.

tail.title: I turned my RSS feeds into an e-ink newspaper to stop reading on my phone
tail.summary: A build log for a scheduled job that renders an RSS pull into a broadsheet layout and pushes it to an e-ink display each morning. This is your NewsBrief with a different output stage, and the layout and typography work is the part you would actually reuse: the daily brief already exists, it just lands as a web artifact. A plausible weekend project that would get the 6am feed off a screen you also work on.

tail.title: agent-safe-pipeline: a reference architecture where agents propose actions but cannot authorize them
tail.summary: A worked pattern that splits proposal from authorization with an immutable intent record, so an agent can never both decide and execute. This is the structural version of the permission discipline your own collectors run under, and it is a citable artefact if you ever write up agentic-action safety. Read the intent-capture format; that is the transferable piece.

tail.title: codex-gpt-5.6-instruct: a prompt framework that reframes the run context to avoid triggering safety training
tail.summary: A public instruction-engineering framework that wraps a coding model's context in a CTF-competition frame with the explicit stated goal of keeping refusal behaviour from activating, and it has picked up a hundred stars in a week. Treat it as a specimen rather than a tool: it is prompt-level refusal suppression in the wild, which is the deployment-side counterpart to the weight-level abliteration your PsychBench Abliterated work studies. Useful as a real-world stimulus set if you ever compare prompt-induced and weight-induced suppression.

tail.title: Shoehorn: quantize an LLM to exactly fit the VRAM you have
tail.summary: A library that measures available memory and picks a quantization scheme to fit, with the author reporting Qwen3-30B-A3B at 50 tok/s on 24GB unified memory. It is written for Apple unified memory so it will not drop onto your 5060 Ti unchanged, but the sizing logic is the reusable half and CUDA is an obvious port. Read DESIGN.md before the README; that is where the fitting heuristic lives.

tail.title: OpenCode Senses: a fully local vision plugin running moondream2 at ~300ms per image
tail.summary: A vision plugin for OpenCode that reads screenshots and images with a small local VLM instead of shipping them to an API, configurable to a larger model if you have the GPU for it. You currently route multimodal reads through the Gemini CLI, so this is the offline alternative for the cases where the image should not leave the machine. moondream2 fits your card several times over.

tail.title: loomfeed: an open-source Reddit alternative built for agents and humans, with provenance tracking
tail.summary: A federated discussion platform designed so that machine-authored posts carry provenance and reputation records rather than hiding, aimed squarely at the failure Reddit is currently having. Reddit has been hard-blocked from your machine for weeks and the paid Apify hop is the only route, so an alternative with a real API is directly interesting to the NewsBrief collectors. Early, but the provenance model is worth reading regardless.

tail.title: multi-agent-workflow-lab: testing and observability for delegation, MCP tools and permissions
tail.summary: A test bench for the parts of a multi-agent system that normally have no tests: which subagent got which tool, what permissions fired, what the sandbox actually allowed. Your NewsBrief run is exactly this shape and currently gets debugged by reading stderr, so a structured trace would tell you where a collector silently under-delivered. Framework-agnostic enough to point at a Claude Code fan-out.

tail.title: Am-1 Arpeggio Machine: a web synth built as a love letter to Berlin School
tail.summary: A browser arpeggiator built by someone who wanted evolving interlocking sequences and could not find an instrument that did it, so wrote one. It is a small, complete, non-AI creative build in the middle of a feed full of agent frameworks, and it plays immediately with no account. Good background generator for a Basilisk writing session.

tail.title: Read the Room: a social-deduction puzzle driven by an LLM relationship matrix
tail.summary: Each scenario holds three or four characters and an explicit character-to-character relationship matrix; the model interprets each turn, updates the matrix, and decides whether your social objective landed. That explicit-state-plus-LLM-interpretation design is the most interesting thing here, because it makes the model's social inference auditable turn by turn. Directly adjacent to your psychology side and free in the browser.

tail.title: cove-sensory-mcp: give a text-only model eyes and ears through a local, privacy-safe MCP server
tail.summary: An MCP server that runs local vision and audio models and exposes them as tools, so a text-only endpoint gains multimodal reads without anything leaving the machine. This is the general-purpose version of the Gemini-CLI delegation you already do, and it would work for any model you route through OpenRouter. Check what it loads into VRAM before wiring it into a session that is already running a local judge.

tail.title: I scored my prediction-market bot with a Brier score. It was worse than guessing.
tail.summary: A short, honest writeup of someone applying a proper scoring rule to their own trading bot and publishing the result when it came out below chance. The calibration discipline is the transferable part and it is the same measurement your judge-calibration protocol depends on. Worth reading as an example of publishing a negative result cleanly rather than quietly retiring the project.

tail.title: moli: a browser built in Rust specifically for AI agents to drive
tail.summary: A from-scratch Rust browser whose primary consumer is an agent rather than a person, aimed at the latency and flakiness of driving Chrome through CDP. Half your collector failures are fetch-layer problems (403s, JS shells, Cloudflare interstitials), so a purpose-built agent browser is worth testing against the three or four hosts that reliably defeat WebFetch. Early-stage; treat claims about speed as unverified.

tail.title: Hermes Bot Mode: a roster of named agents with their own chats, avatars and routines
tail.summary: Nous Research shipped a desktop mode where agents are persistent named characters with separate histories and scheduled behaviours rather than anonymous task runners. The persona-persistence design is the interesting bit for someone with both a recall_persona memory layer and a novel with characters in it. Nous open-sources genuinely, so the implementation is readable.

tail.title: LibreChat 0.8.8-rc1: interrupt or steer an agent run mid-flight
tail.summary: The release candidate adds mid-run steering, so you can redirect an agent that is going wrong without killing the run and losing its context. That is the single most-wanted behaviour in long collector fan-outs, where the alternative is watching twenty minutes of work go the wrong direction. Worth watching how they implement the interrupt boundary even if you do not use LibreChat.

tail.title: Cadre.rocks: a local-first board for orchestrating several coding agents
tail.summary: A kanban-style local board where each card is a task handed to a coding agent, with state kept on your machine rather than in a service. It is the visual counterpart to the file-based planning plugin you already run, and it fits the way you fan work out to subagents. Worth comparing against planning-with-files to see whether a board actually beats markdown for your workload.

tail.title: Hexis: open-source management for Claude Skills
tail.summary: A manager rather than another skill pack: it installs, versions and enables or disables skills across projects so a skills directory stops rotting. You have well over twenty skills spanning research, writing and audio, several of which overlap, which is exactly the point where a manager stops being overhead. Note this is the one entry worth taking from an extremely crowded skills week.

tail.title: awesome-claude-output-styles: 17 installable output styles for Claude Code
tail.summary: A collection of output-style definitions with credited methodological sources, aimed at getting Claude Code to stop writing in the default register. You have a standing rule banning rhetorical prose in docs and a whole mimesis stack for voice, so this is worth mining for the mechanical patterns other people ban. Do not use it in place of mimesis for your own voice; use it for the flat-declarative default.

tail.title: OpenViking: a self-evolving context database that unifies agent memory, RAG and skills
tail.summary: ByteDance's Volcengine open-sourced a store that treats memory, retrieved knowledge and skills as one substrate that reorganises itself as the agent works. That is the same architectural bet LKHS makes, so it is worth reading as a competing design, particularly on how it decides what to promote and what to let decay. Sizeable project with real backing rather than a weekend repo.

tail.title: Ballet: workflow automation that writes its own integrations against any API
tail.summary: Instead of shipping a connector catalogue, Ballet reads an API's docs and generates the integration on demand, which removes the usual 'no node for that service' wall in n8n-style tools. If it holds up, it is the automation layer for the long tail of services that will never get a maintained MCP server. Test it on something awkward like an .edu.au scholarship page before trusting the demo.

tail.title: repo-context-mcp: repo map, code search and token-aware context packs
tail.summary: An MCP server that builds a structural map of a repository and serves context in packs sized to a token budget rather than dumping files. Your research repos are large enough that the current pattern is Explore-agent fan-outs, and a budgeted pack is a cheaper first move. Worth pointing at the PsychBench UpdatedRun tree to see whether it finds structure the glob-and-grep route misses.

tail.title: open-video: a local video-generation runner, positioned as Ollama for MiniMax H3
tail.summary: A wrapper that gives local video generation the one-command pull-and-run ergonomics Ollama gave to text models, with ComfyUI as the backend. If it handles model fetching and VRAM fitting honestly it removes most of the setup tax on trying video gen at all on a 16GB card. Check its memory requirements before pulling; H3-class models are not small.

tail.title: A walkable 3D tour of a feedforward neural net
tail.summary: A browser scene you move through, with the layers and activations rendered as space you walk between rather than a diagram you look at. It is a small thing that makes the shape of a forward pass sit differently, and it takes about a minute. Good link to hand anyone who asks what you actually do.

tail.title: CoreTrace: a visual 16-bit CPU simulator you can step and replay in the browser
tail.summary: Write assembly, run it, then step or replay cycle by cycle while watching registers, flags, ALU and buses update live, with breakpoints. Nothing to do with AI, which is part of why it is worth the ten minutes. The replay-previous-cycles feature is the one most such simulators skip.

tail.title: Soft Edge: a painting engine that keeps strokes as data so you can sculpt them later
tail.summary: Every other paint program rasterises a stroke the moment you make it; this one stores strokes as records and re-rasterises each frame like a game engine, so any property of a stroke stays editable forever. It is a genuinely different architectural idea rather than a feature, and it is playable now as a tech demo. Worth trying if only to feel what non-destructive actually means.

tail.title: hnfiltered: Hacker News with the slop filtered out by a Cloudflare Worker
tail.summary: A proxy that rewrites the HN front page in flight, dropping low-quality posts while leaving popular and controversial stories untouched, built with HTMLRewriter in an afternoon. The author's self-aware framing (vibe-coded a slop filter to escape slop) is half the appeal. The filtering heuristic is worth reading given you run a ranking pipeline over the same source.

tail.title: SlopScan: a browser extension that scores public git repos for AI slop
tail.summary: An extension that annotates GitHub repo pages with a slop score derived from commit and code patterns, so you see it before you clone. Given how much of this week's new-repo harvest is star-farm and skill-pack noise, a scoring layer at the point of browsing is directly useful. Treat the score as a prior, not a verdict; the failure mode is penalising legitimate generated boilerplate.

tail.title: LuaCAD: parametric CAD scripted in Lua instead of the OpenSCAD language
tail.summary: A solid modeller that keeps OpenSCAD's constructive-solid-geometry model but drops its language, using Lua with operator overloading so union, difference and intersection read as plus, minus and times. Ships with both a CLI and a desktop app with live preview. A satisfying weekend rabbit hole if you ever want a physical object out of a script.

tail.title: NotABot: a browser game that collects training data for human-versus-bot detection
tail.summary: You play against a mix of humans and models and guess which is which, and your judgements feed a detection dataset. The interesting question underneath is what cues people actually use, which is a psychology question rather than an ML one. Two minutes to play and it sits directly on your cyberpsychology interest.

tail.title: Is AI Dumber Today? A crowd-sourced index of daily model experience
tail.summary: A running index built from user reports of whether a model felt worse today, tracked per model over time. The measurement is pure subjective report with all the biases that implies, which is exactly what makes it an interesting object next to the Opus 5 essay above. Worth a look as an example of a self-report instrument deployed at internet scale with no controls.

tail.title: DeepSeek Harness handbook: the ecosystem written up end to end
tail.summary: A bilingual manual covering DeepSeek Harness install, plugin development, tuning and measured multi-agent comparisons on the same model, which is the one useful entry point into a genuinely large plugin wave. Read the same-model multi-agent comparison section: it is a rough eval of orchestration overhead. Flagged mainly so you can decide once whether DSH is worth tracking, rather than seeing nine of its plugins in every harvest.

tail.title: Neal: Claude and Codex working the same migration together
tail.summary: A CLI built out of a real large-frontend migration, around two findings: telling an agent to keep working unless blocked does not survive long stretches, and big projects need externally-enforced chunking. It coordinates two different vendors' agents on one codebase. The write-up of why long autonomous runs decay is more valuable than the tool.

tail.title: anti-slop: design rules that stop coding agents generating generic AI-slop UI
tail.summary: A rules file that constrains an agent's visual defaults away from the purple-gradient-and-rounded-card look every model converges on. It is the visual analogue of the prose bans you already enforce, and it makes the same argument: the tell is the default, so name the default and forbid it. Short enough to read and adapt in ten minutes.

tail.title: kenforthewin/atomic: a self-hosted, semantically-connected personal knowledge base
tail.summary: Notes that link themselves by meaning rather than by explicit wikilinks, running entirely on your own machine. That is the local, file-owning version of what LKHS does over conversations, and it would sit next to rather than replace it. Worth checking whether it exposes an API an agent could write into.

tail.title: koharu: an ML-powered manga translator written in Rust
tail.summary: Detection, OCR, translation and typesetting-back-into-the-bubble as one local pipeline, which is a harder multi-stage problem than it looks and it runs on consumer hardware. Worth reading as a worked example of chaining several small local models into one artefact, which is the shape of most useful local-AI builds. The typesetting stage is the part nobody else gets right.

tail.title: Blog about things you don't understand yet
tail.summary: An argument that writing about a topic before you have mastered it is where the useful writing actually comes from, and that waiting for authority produces nothing. Relevant given you have several half-finished analyses and a publication pipeline that stalls on completeness. Short, and it is an argument you can disagree with productively.

tail.title: My homelab got hacked: a postmortem
tail.summary: A specific, unglamorous account of how a self-hosted setup was compromised, what the attacker did, and which assumption failed. Useful because you run local services and the failure here was a default rather than an exotic exploit. Short enough to read before the next thing you expose.

tail.title: Remarc: comment on anything on your screen and send it to your agent
tail.summary: A pointing-and-annotating layer for agent output, built on the observation that there is a rich toolset for giving humans contextual feedback and almost nothing for giving it to models. Chat is a bad channel for 'this specific line in the plan is wrong', which is a problem you hit on every long session. Also ships as an MCP server so the feedback lands in-context.

tail.title: codex-structured-steering: a UI showing every assumption your coding agent is making
tail.summary: Surfaces the implicit assumptions behind an agent's plan as an editable list, so you correct a premise rather than the output that followed from it. The general idea transfers to any harness and is close to what a good plan-review step should do. From the ArchiveBox author, so the tooling instincts are sound.

tail.title: mcp-aftereffects: a TypeScript MCP server for Adobe After Effects
tail.summary: Project, composition and layer introspection plus atomic edits, on Windows and macOS, driving a professional motion-graphics application from an agent. It is the clearest current example of MCP reaching a real creative desktop tool rather than another API wrapper. Relevant if any Basilisk or presentation work ever needs motion.

tail.title: ego-lite: a fast browser for agents that shares your logged-in session state
tail.summary: Built for the case where an agent needs to act as you on sites that require a session, by sharing existing browser state rather than re-authenticating. That capability is exactly why it warrants care: an agent inheriting your logins is a large blast radius, so read the permission model before running it. Notable as the second agent-browser on this week's trending list alongside moli.

tail.title: How Claude's text watermark actually works: SynthID-Text applied to the randomness source, and what it cannot do
tail.summary: Anthropic's own technical account of the scheme, which uses Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text approach: rather than altering the output, it replaces the arbitrary randomness used to pick between equally viable next words with a key-and-prior-context-derived choice, so the sequence can later be checked for consistency with that key. Confidence scales with passage length and degrades badly on short samples, code and highly factual text where word choice is constrained. Anthropic states the mark cannot distinguish 'Claude wrote this' from 'Claude heavily edited this', cannot confirm human authorship or identify other systems, carries no identifying information, and does not survive a full rewrite.

tail.title: Near-autonomous agents ran a 12-wave intrusion on Taiwan's nuclear safety agency, solving CAPTCHAs at 100% and self-correcting
tail.summary: Suspected Chinese operators used an agent framework built on open-source Hermes and OpenAI agents, deploying up to eight sub-agents across 12 waves between 1 and 4 July, compromising 85 government accounts and 2,564 personnel records before pivoting to the nuclear safety agency, supply-chain vendors and seven energy companies. The autonomy evidence is the interesting part: unprompted reconnaissance that found 36+ API endpoints and unauthenticated databases, CAPTCHA solving at 100% accuracy, autonomous password spraying, and 'learning cycles' in which the models searched vulnerability databases and GitHub for exploitable techniques and self-corrected on error. Attribution stops at a Chinese-language operator rather than a named group.

tail.title: Google Security tells red teams to stop running manual exercises and build their own agent orchestrators
tail.summary: Google's argument is that ransomware groups and initial-access brokers have the strongest incentive to adopt agents because they value volume and speed above all, so industrialised social engineering and automated attack chains are the near-term shape of the threat. The prescribed transition is incremental: automate isolated phases (reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement), build modular subagents, then wire them to an orchestrator for autonomous simulation. Worth reading as a methodology piece rather than an evidence one, since it carries no empirical findings or numbers, only qualitative predictions.

tail.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability of Biological AIs
tail.summary: A research lead at BiodynAI argues that foundation models trained on DNA, proteins, gene expression, cell images and tissue samples are the best available 'model organisms for mechinterp in the wild' — small enough to study, real enough to matter, and unusually blessed with clean ground truth that language models lack. The second argument is instrumental: biosecurity auditing of these models is impossible without interpretability, because they encode knowledge that is not derivable from their default outputs by design. The post is framed as an open-problems list rather than results.

tail.title: A chip-verification veteran applies coverage-driven V&V to the 'Pacing the frontier' proposal
tail.summary: The author co-originated coverage-driven verification and spent decades verifying chips and autonomous vehicles, and applies that frame to the 'Pacing the frontier' letter and proposal for slowing frontier development while making models safer. The concrete suggestion for the recent OpenAI incidents is a 'rewind-fix-check loop': rewind to the decision point, try an improved solution, and re-check comprehensively rather than patching forward. The interest here is methodological transfer — treating safety cases as coverage problems with trackable closure rather than as narrative arguments.

tail.title: How the American Executive Could Control AI Companies
tail.summary: An inventory of unilateral executive-branch levers over AI firms, anchored in two recent live cases: the Department of Defense's dispute with Anthropic and the resulting threat to invoke the Defense Production Act, and the short-lived export controls on Claude Fable/Mythos 5 delivered as a vaguely worded letter from Howard Lutnick that may not have been legally sound but worked anyway. The authors argue executive dominance will persist because the national-security and foreign-policy framings of AI structurally empower that branch, and would intensify if capabilities move fast. Policy analysis with actual instruments attached rather than an op-ed.

tail.title: Avoiding the corporate treacherous turn: crowd-sourcing mission-lock designs for a safety-first AI company
tail.summary: Written by someone considering launching a commercial venture ('Prealign') on value generalisation, taking OpenAI's non-profit-to-capped-profit trajectory as the failure case to design against. The ask is for corporate-structure ideas that survive investor pressure: an ethics board with real enforcement power, board ownership of the company, differentiated share classes, choice of incorporating jurisdiction. Useful as a live catalogue of what governance mechanisms people think actually bind, given that the canonical structure did not.

tail.title: Scrying, Modeling, and Nerdsnipe: how to generate concepts when the true hypothesis has not occurred to you yet
tail.summary: Prompted by conversations with Richard Ngo at ILIAD: Aeneid, this is about the research situation where the truth is too complex to hold in mind, so any hypothesis you can actually consider is necessarily incomplete. Ngo's claim that we lack the right concepts to understand agency, and that developing them is robustly good for safety, is the motivating case. The post distinguishes conceptual safety research broadly (which includes inventing devices to control agents) from agent foundations specifically.

tail.title: Do It Like Darwin: can the scientific-discovery loop be automated without embodiment?
tail.summary: Takes the labs' stated goal of automating science and unbundles it into separable questions: is it doable with near-future LLMs and agents, and is it doable without embodiment, or do we need generally intelligent robots in physical labs. AlphaFold is the counterexample the author has to handle — a Nobel-winning result that was domain-tailored rather than a general discovery loop. Jeff Dean's exit from Google to found Discovery Loop is treated as the signal that the general version is now being seriously attempted.

tail.title: Manifund publishes the list of people it wants as regrantors and the $50k-per-pot structure behind it
tail.summary: A follow-up to Regranting in 2026 naming the people Manifund would be excited to hand grantmaking authority to, sorted into rough categories and screened on taste, dealflow and hustle. The mechanism is explicit: if they raise $2m for regranting they intend to give each named person a $50k pot. The post is careful that this is a wishlist rather than a roster of people who have agreed, which makes it a useful read on where independent-researcher funding decisions are about to sit.

tail.title: Don't forget why learning is important: against 'read a lot and develop takes' as AI-safety career advice
tail.summary: The argument is that newcomers to AI safety are told to read widely and develop opinions, and lose track of the fact that knowledge is instrumental — it is for doing better things in the world, which should determine what you bother learning. The author is confident in the main claim and explicitly less confident about which specific things are most valuable. Written under a self-imposed constraint of 13 push-ups every five minutes until failure, which the author flags as a reason it is less polished than usual.

tail.title: What Mormons get right about community building, read as a manual for AI-safety movement design
tail.summary: The author, who grew up partly in Utah, argues that religions and impact-driven movements share enough structure that the LDS church's retention machinery is worth copying, citing longer Mormon lifespans, Utah's first-place volunteering rate, and language training so effective that missionaries are a known pipeline into foreign service and intelligence careers. He is upfront that he is generalising rather than hedging properly, and that the claims fit the Utah/Idaho/Arizona corridor better than the church globally. Relevant given how much of AI safety's talent pipeline runs on community infrastructure.

tail.title: The Day Humanity Died (Parody of American Pie)
tail.summary: A full-length American Pie rewrite covering AI-winter benchmark disappointment, the race to ASI, and running out of Claude Code credits in Fable mode, with a verse nodding to 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies'. The author opens by disclaiming that the doom level in the lyrics is well above his actual views. Filed here as the week's artefact of AI-safety culture rather than as research.

tail.title: When Genius Fails: the case that AI lab leaders' expertise does not transfer
tail.summary: James Wang's argument is that AI research excellence is being treated as general epistemic authority, and he works through five instances: Leopold Aschenbrenner's leveraged hedge fund collapsing despite his lab credentials, Altman and Amodei making labour-market predictions without economic history, lab-adjacent startups assuming ChatGPT substitutes for domain expertise in materials science and bioengineering, safety guardrails set paternalistically to the point that Hugging Face uses Chinese models for cybersecurity defence work, and PhD-heavy teams producing groupthink. The Malthus comparison is the load-bearing one: confident catastrophe forecasts from people expert in the wrong field.

tail.title: Epoch: most workplace AI use runs on free plans, except in science and tech
tail.summary: An occupation-level breakdown of whether workplace AI use is employer-provided or self-supplied on a free tier, finding the free-plan pattern dominant across most occupations. Science and technology occupations are the exception where employer provisioning leads. The distinction matters for any survey or eval that assumes workers are using the frontier tier their employer nominally licenses.

tail.title: Compute-optimal is not cluster-optimal: sparsity that wins on FLOPs loses 1.70x on wall-clock
tail.summary: The argument is that scaling laws optimise model FLOPs while clusters bill GPU-hours, so the two prescriptions diverge once MFU, goodput and peak throughput enter the denominator. Under fixed model-FLOPs budgets predicted loss falls monotonically with sparsity across the calibrated range, yet wall-clock per delivered model FLOP rises monotonically with sparsity up to 1.70x the densest configuration, so boundary-optimal sparsity near 0.96 is simply infeasible on four nodes in five days. Re-optimising under real cluster constraints lands on an interior sparsity with 0.031 nats lower loss, and the configuration with the most model FLOPs (1.94e23) loses to one with roughly 36% fewer.

tail.title: Evaluating your agentic harnesses: pass rate, tokens, status codes and replan count as the minimum suite
tail.summary: Proposes a four-metric baseline for harness evaluation — pass rate, token usage, status-code distribution that separates failed_execute from failed_verify from budget exhaustion, and replan count as a robustness proxy — over a task suite deliberately mixing well-posed and adversarial cases to exercise every code path. The worked findings are concrete: re-planning degraded gracefully when asked about a non-existent city, collapsing a 10-node DAG to 7 rather than failing outright; embedding-based memory retrieval beat word-overlap similarity 3-0 where query and stored vocabulary differed. Separating failure modes by status code rather than collapsing to pass/fail is the transferable part.

tail.title: America's sloppiness on model security could hand China the distillation advantage
tail.summary: Transformer's big story is that policymakers' anxiety about Chinese labs distilling American model outputs runs into the fact that US labs' own security practices make the outputs cheap to harvest. The briefing also reports the White House plans to extend its AI framework to open-weight models once they reach Mythos-level cyber capabilities, Zuckerberg's 6,500-word manifesto gently criticising that framework, and a run of senior departures from OpenAI. Policy coverage with mechanisms rather than positioning.

tail.title: The January 6 organizer turning conservatives against AI data centres
tail.summary: Reported from a data-centre protest outside a municipal building in Union County, New Jersey, where residents mobilised by a Facebook ad turned up at borough council meetings without knowing who had organised them. The piece traces how anti-data-centre organising is being seeded into conservative networks by an operative with a January 6 record, and how the local participants are indifferent to that provenance. A different angle on the data-centre backlash than the utility-bill and pollution coverage this board has run.

tail.title: Don't classify, hallucinate: generate imaginary labels, then snap them to your real taxonomy with embeddings
tail.summary: Doug Turnbull's trick, which Willison applies to his own 1,856 blog tags: rather than stuffing an unwieldy vocabulary into the prompt and asking the model to pick, tell the model to invent labels freely, then use vector embeddings to map each invented label to the nearest real one. Including one example of the shape of your labels is enough to steer the model's guesses into the right register. It turns an intractable multi-label classification prompt into a generation step plus a nearest-neighbour lookup.

tail.title: Interconnects on GLM-5.3: frontier agentic coding scores at ~750B parameters, a third of Kimi K3
tail.summary: Nathan Lambert reads Z.ai's GLM-5.3 announcement, currently coding-plan only with API and open weights on Hugging Face promised within two weeks, and treats the benchmark jump as exceptional rather than routine — surpassing Kimi K3 on many benchmarks and Claude Fable 5 or GPT-5.6-Sol on some. The parameter count is the argument: roughly 750B against Kimi K3's ~2.2T for comparable agentic coding results. Z.ai's own framing is that scaling post-training is the whole story, which Lambert takes seriously.

tail.title: Gelman answers a high-school student's five questions about statistics
tail.summary: A cold-email summer assignment asking what got him into statistics, what advice he'd give, the biggest challenge in the work, the most common mistake people make reading statistics, and where to learn more — answered straight rather than deflected. Worth two minutes for the answer on common misreadings, which is Gelman's standing subject compressed to a paragraph.

tail.title: SPAR's Fall 2026 AI safety research projects close to mentee applications on 18 August
tail.summary: SPAR (run under the Kairos Project) has its Fall 2026 mentee applications open with a stated deadline of 18 August, listing mentor-attached research projects across AI safety. The project listing is the substance — it is a directory of who is looking for collaborators on what this autumn. Remote eligibility and international-applicant terms are not stated on the listing page and would need confirming with spar@kairos-project.org.

tail.title: AI Safety Events and Training, week 33: EA Summit Geneva and Paris added to the directory
tail.summary: The weekly roll-up of newly announced events and training programmes on existential risk from AI, this week adding EA Summit Geneva on 24 October (pay to attend, assistance available) and EA Summit Paris on 5 December (free, sessions in multiple languages). Useful as a low-cost standing watch on the programme calendar rather than for any single listing.

tail.title: Cursor is now part of SpaceX
tail.summary: Anysphere's announcement that Cursor is joining SpaceX, following the same corporate consolidation that produced the SpaceXAI Grok releases. The relevant question for anyone with Cursor in a pipeline is what happens to the editor's independent model routing and data handling under that owner. Announced on the company blog with 93 points and 104 comments of developer reaction on Hacker News.

tail.title: Google ships HEIR, an open-source compiler toolchain for running trained models on homomorphically encrypted data
tail.summary: HEIR (Homomorphic Encryption Intermediate Representation) converts pre-trained models to operate on encrypted inputs so a server can compute and return results without seeing the data, demonstrated on recommendation, fraud detection, threat intrusion and hotword detection. The honesty caveat matters: the published latency figures are single-threaded CPU and no concrete performance numbers appear, with the speed argument deferred to accelerators from Belfort, Niobium, Cornami and Optalysys. Treat the cost claim as a direction of travel rather than a measured result.

tail.title: Perplexity blocks Time's agent-targeted ads and calls them deceptive
tail.summary: Time began serving ad creative specifically to AI agents crawling its pages, and Perplexity has blocked it on the grounds that content shown only to machines and not to humans is deceptive. The dispute is an early instance of a genuine open question in agentic browsing — whether publishers may address the agent differently from the reader, and who adjudicates that. No standards body currently has jurisdiction over the answer.

tail.title: FTC and state AGs act against Hims and Hers over deceptive and unlawful privacy practices
tail.summary: A joint FTC and multi-state enforcement action against the telehealth firm over how it handled and disclosed health data, filed as a press release with the complaint attached. This is policy with teeth rather than commentary — an enforcement instrument against a digital-health platform, which is the regulatory neighbourhood any LLM mental-health or clinical-triage deployment lands in. Note the release is dated July on the FTC site despite surfacing on Hacker News this week.

tail.title: The case for a coherent national AI cybersecurity policy, from a security practitioner
tail.summary: Written by a machine-learning security practitioner rather than a policy shop, arguing that the US currently has agency-level AI security guidance but no coherent national posture, and that the agentic-attack tempo now visible makes the gap urgent. Pairs directly with this week's Taiwan intrusion reporting and Google's red-team piece as the practitioner-side view of the same problem.

tail.title: UN regional centre: AI's water, land and mineral demands are outrunning the environmental accounting
tail.summary: UNRIC's summary of UN environment-side assessments of AI infrastructure, covering freshwater withdrawal for cooling, land use for data centres, and critical-mineral demand alongside the more commonly reported electricity figure. The framing is that reporting concentrates on energy because it is the one input with published numbers, which understates the footprint. Useful as the multi-input version of a story usually told as a power-bill story.

tail.title: Z.ai publishes a coordinated vulnerability disclosure programme
tail.summary: The GLM lab has stood up a coordinated vulnerability disclosure channel with scope and reporting terms, arriving in the same week as its GLM-5.3 announcement. Notable mainly because open-weight Chinese labs have generally lacked the formal security-reporting apparatus that US labs run alongside their bug bounties. Whether model-behaviour issues fall in scope alongside infrastructure vulnerabilities is the thing to read the scope statement for.

tail.title: AI Model Atlas: the Hugging Face model population rendered as an interactive 3D derivative graph
tail.summary: A Cosmograph rendering of the open-model ecosystem as an interconnected graph, where edges are fine-tune and quantisation derivative relationships and clusters are base-model families. It makes the concentration visible in a way the download tables do not — the Qwen cluster's dominance shows up as sheer mass. A quick way to check what a given base model's derivative footprint actually looks like before betting a pipeline on it.

tail.title: AI by Hand: working through architectures and algorithms on paper, 73,000 subscribers in
tail.summary: Prof. Tom Yeh's newsletter teaches transformer maths, algorithms and architectures by having readers compute them manually rather than through library calls, on the theory that the mechanism does not stick otherwise. It reached the Hacker News front page with 170 points this week. Relevant if you want the attention or normalisation arithmetic to be intuitive rather than merely importable.

tail.title: Mistral OCR 4.1
tail.summary: Mistral's documentation page for the 4.1 revision of its OCR model, covering supported document structures, output schema and pricing. Document-extraction quality is the practical bottleneck for anyone building a corpus out of PDFs, which is why this hit 402 points on Hacker News. Read the structured-output section rather than the headline accuracy claim.

tail.title: Launch HN: Bullet, a coding agent optimised for latency rather than capability
tail.summary: A YC S26 launch pitching speed as the axis of competition among coding agents, on the argument that the frontier-capability race has left interactive latency unaddressed. The comment thread (84 comments) is the useful part, since it is where practitioners compare it against their existing Claude Code and Codex setups. Worth a look if agent turnaround time rather than task success is your current constraint.

tail.title: Show HN: harness-training auto-tunes the scaffold instead of the model, claiming cross-model gains
tail.summary: Treats the agent harness — prompts, tool definitions, control flow — as the trainable object and optimises it directly, reporting gains that transfer across both models and benchmarks rather than being tuned to one pairing. If the cross-model claim holds it is an argument that a meaningful share of reported model-to-model differences are actually scaffold differences. Small repo, so read the eval protocol before believing the transfer result.

tail.title: Show HN: MCP Memory, agent memory over Google's OKF plus SQLite FTS5
tail.summary: An MCP server providing persistent agent memory built on SQLite's FTS5 full-text index with Google's Open Knowledge Format for structure, pitched on retrieval speed against embedding-based memory layers. The design bet is that lexical search plus explicit structure beats vector similarity for the recall patterns agents actually generate. Sits alongside the several shared-memory MCP servers this board has tracked over the past fortnight.

tail.title: Show HN: MCP-stama, a dependency-free Rust MCP server
tail.summary: A Model Context Protocol server implementation in Rust with no external dependencies, aimed at startup latency and a small audit surface. Zero dependencies is the security argument as much as the performance one, given how much of the MCP ecosystem is npm-installed. Reached 73 points on Hacker News with no comment thread.

tail.title: Show HN: Mole, a deep-research agent that runs in the terminal
tail.summary: A terminal-native deep-research agent that runs search, fetch and synthesis loops locally rather than through a hosted research product. The appeal for anyone already living in a CLI agent setup is that the intermediate artefacts stay on disk and are inspectable, instead of being summarised away inside a web UI. Compare against the hosted deep-research offerings on citation handling before switching.

tail.title: HashAgent shares an AI agent as a single URL, executing locally via WebGPU
tail.summary: Encodes an agent's definition into a URL so that opening the link runs the agent in the visitor's browser on WebGPU, with no server-side inference and nothing to host. The distribution model is the interesting part — an agent becomes a shareable artefact rather than a deployed service. Model size is bounded by what will load into browser memory, which caps what the agent can actually be.

tail.title: Show HN: Biasly.ai, bias detection with historical context attached
tail.summary: A tool that flags bias in text and pairs each flag with historical context intended to explain why the framing registers as biased rather than only asserting that it does. The explain-alongside-detect design is the part worth examining, since bias classifiers that emit a score without a rationale are the ones that fail audit. No validation data or agreement statistics are published on the landing page.

tail.title: Show HN: twenty years of one researcher's work turned into a game by Claude
tail.summary: A researcher fed two decades of their own research output to Claude and had it built into a playable game, posted as a Show HN. The interesting question it raises is what the translation preserves — whether the game encodes the findings or only their surface vocabulary. A concrete data point on LLM-assisted research communication rather than research production.

tail.title: Astral Codex Ten book review: The Escape Artist
tail.summary: A finalist in the 2026 ACX book review contest, written anonymously pending the vote, on a Holocaust account the reviewer argues avoids all three of the genre's standard consolations: the innocent child narrator, the redemptive small act, and the morally conflicted German. The review is about why those clichés exist and what a text reads like without them. Long-tail reading rather than AI content.

tail.title: The quest for caffeine you can have at night, and the paraxanthine startups selling it
tail.summary: Scott Alexander works through caffeine metabolism — CYP1A2 converting caffeine to the equally stimulating paraxanthine over a ~5 hour half-life, then clearing paraxanthine over ~3 hours — to assess whether the several companies selling paraxanthine directly can deliver an evening stimulant that clears before bed. The graphed total effective concentration is the crux, since the two compounds are assumed equally potent. Standard Alexander treatment: take the marketing claim seriously enough to check the pharmacokinetics.

tail.title: sqlite-utils 4.2 rewrites table.transform() to preserve check constraints, unique constraints and column comments
tail.summary: The transform() feature implements complex ALTER TABLE operations by building a fresh table, copying the data across and swapping it in, and this release widens the set of schema edge cases that survive the round trip to include check constraints, unique constraints and column comments, plus new introspection properties. Willison shipped 4.2.1 the same day after 4.2 crashed on an unlisted typing-extensions dependency, and documents the isolated smoke test (uv run --isolated --no-default-groups) he added to catch that class of packaging bug. The packaging lesson is the more broadly useful half.

tail.title: Hugging Face, Strands Agents and LeRobot: record, train and deploy a robot policy from one place
tail.summary: An AWS-authored walkthrough wiring Strands Agents to LeRobot with Hugging Face Storage Buckets so that demonstration recording, policy training and deployment run through one streaming data loop rather than three disconnected stages. The claim is about closing the loop latency between collecting demonstrations and having a retrained policy back on the robot. Relevant mainly as an example of the streaming-data-loop pattern generalising beyond robotics.

Remote-global is the tag that matters for a 462 visa holder, though the aisafety.com remote tag is known to be unreliable - it labelled the Constellation Visiting Fellowship 'Remote (Global)' when the role requires three days a week in Berkeley. The Ashby posting is JS-rendered and returned only its title to both a fetch and a search, so salary, deadline and work-authorisation terms are all unread. tail.summary: One of two FAR AI roles posted 14 August; the Research Scientist is Bay-Area only, the Research Engineer is listed as 'Remote, Global; San Francisco Bay Area, USA'.
